records.summary: The property at 1152 Taylor St is in the RM-3 (Residential-Mixed, Medium Density) zoning district, where restaurants are not a principally permitted use; the Planning Code table has no restaurant row, and retail uses read as not permitted on the first story. However, the site history shows an active Type 41 ABC license (beer and wine, eating place) issued in 1981 to Nob Hill Cafe at 1148 & 1152 Taylor St, currently in "REV PENDING" status, suggesting an existing restaurant use that may qualify under Limited Corner Commercial Use provisions (§231) or continuation of existing use. Within 500 feet there are only 2 registered food/drink businesses and 3 ABC licenses, indicating low density. Recent precedent within 1,000 feet shows Planning approved three restaurant referrals at 1257 Taylor St (112 m away, same RM-3 zoning) in 2022-2023 for a new restaurant, noting the use is "not permitted" but approving ABC licenses anyway, likely under continuation or limited commercial use exceptions.

patterns.pattern: Restaurants in RM-3 zoning are consistently approved by Planning only as 'continuation of existing use' under §186 or as 'Limited Corner Commercial Use' under §231, never as principally permitted uses, because Planning Code §209.2 does not list restaurants in the RM-3 use table.

Planning explicitly prohibits expansion of non-conforming restaurant uses in RM-3: the 2022 and 2023 approvals at 1257 Taylor both state 'may not expand' and cite non-conforming use restrictions in §§180-183.

Abandonment for three years extinguishes non-conforming status: Planning's 2022-2023 decisions at 1257 Taylor warned that if the space 'has been discontinued or abandoned for a period of three years,' the use would lose non-conforming protection and have to comply with current RM-3 zoning (which prohibits restaurants).

When a restaurant is not a continuation or corner-commercial use, Planning requires a Conditional Use Authorization in RM-3: the 2015 CUA at 1030 Washington St (269 m away) approved a new restaurant via discretionary hearing, taking six months from filing to approval.
Once a CUA is granted for a restaurant in RM-3, subsequent permits (health, ABC) cite the CUA motion number and treat the use as a Limited Commercial Use under §186 for ongoing operations.

Limited Corner Commercial Use under §231 may allow restaurants in RM-3 on corner lots without the 'may not expand' restriction that applies to §186 continuations, as shown by the 2023 approval at 1098 Jackson St.

Agency referrals (ABC, health) for restaurants in RM-3 are routinely approved within days or weeks when the use is already established or qualifies under §186/§231, but the underlying zoning entitlement question must be resolved first.

findings.text: Zoning district RM-3 does not list restaurants as principally permitted; the table row for Retail Sales and Service Uses reads not permitted on the first story per Planning Code §209.2 as of June 2023.

A Type 41 ABC license (on-sale beer and wine, eating place) was issued to Nob Hill Cafe at 1148 & 1152 Taylor St on January 9, 1981, and shows status REV PENDING as of June 26, 2023, indicating a restaurant use was on file at this address.

Planning approved three agency referrals at 1257 Taylor St (112 m away, RM-3 zoning) in 2022–2023 for a new restaurant, each stating restaurants are not permitted in RM-3 but allowing continuation as a Limited Commercial Use per §186 where the prior restaurant closed in 2021 and was not abandoned for three years.

The 2022 and 2023 approvals at 1257 Taylor each state the restaurant 'may not expand' and cite Planning Code §§180–183 restrictions on non-conforming uses; if the space is abandoned for three years it loses non-conforming status and must comply with current RM-3 controls.

A Conditional Use Authorization for a new restaurant in RM-3 was approved at 1030 Washington St (269 m away) in November 2015, filed in May 2015, demonstrating that discretionary approval is available when continuation does not apply.

The description states the space is retail converting to restaurant as an enlargement of the existing restaurant, but no record shows whether the 1981 license remained active or was abandoned, and whether this expansion falls within existing non-conforming boundaries or requires a new use authorization cannot be established from public records.

approvals.summary: A health permit to operate is allowed after plan check and inspection; the permit is issued by the Department of Public Health without a hearing once the facility passes final inspection and a certified food safety manager is on staff.

findings.text: Every food facility needs a health permit to operate, issued by SF Department of Public Health after plan review and inspection, under the California Retail Food Code and San Francisco Health Code Article 8.

The Department of Public Health refers each permit-to-operate application to the Planning Department for zoning review, and the building permit application is also referred to Planning per Planning Code §175.

approvals.summary: A building permit with change of use is further review because tenant improvements with a Planning Code change of use (retail to restaurant) require a permit that must conform to Planning Code before issuance, and whether the change is allowed depends on the zoning determination.

findings.text: Retail to restaurant is a change of use under Planning Code §102 based on the last use of the space as described.
The description states tenant improvements, and any change of use requires a building permit that must conform to Planning Code per §175 before the Department of Building Inspection will issue it.
The occupant load is not stated, so whether the Building Code change of occupancy is from Group B (under 50 persons) to Assembly Group A-2 (50 or more) cannot be established from the description.

Limited cooking is stated; the health plan check fee schedule shows $828 for a small remodel and $2,207 for a new restaurant in FY 2026–27, and the plan check covers kitchen layout, finishes, equipment and menu.

expected_conditions.condition: Restaurant use may not expand beyond the square footage and premises boundaries covered by the original 1981 license if approved as a continuation of non-conforming use under Planning Code §186.
expected_conditions.basis: The 2022 and 2023 approvals at 1257 Taylor St (RM-3, 112 m away) each state 'may not expand' and cite §§180–183 non-conforming use restrictions. Comparable case: Back to Back restaurant was approved as continuation of the Venticello space that closed in 2021, but Planning warned that expansion would require compliance with RM-3 zoning (which prohibits restaurants) or a CUA.

expected_conditions.condition: Operating hours limited to 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. if the use is permitted under Limited Corner Commercial or Limited Commercial provisions, because RM-3 zoning reads hours after 10 p.m. as not principally permitted per §209.2.
expected_conditions.basis: Planning Code §209.2 states P (principally permitted) 06:00–22:00 and NP (not permitted) 22:00–06:00 for Retail Sales and Service Uses in RM-3 as of June 2023. Later hours would require conditional use authorization.

expected_conditions.condition: If approved via Conditional Use Authorization, the Commission may condition the restaurant to operate as incidental to a residential use, limit delivery hours, require a community liaison, and prohibit outdoor amplified sound, based on RM-3 neighborhood context.
expected_conditions.basis: Conditional use findings in residential-mixed districts typically address neighborhood compatibility. The 2015 CUA at 1030 Washington St (RM-3, 269 m away) approved a new restaurant after discretionary review; conditions are not detailed in the brief record but CUAs in RM districts commonly limit hours, deliveries and noise.

expected_conditions.condition: Grease interceptor sized to SFPUC FOG program requirements must be installed and the Installation Verification Form filed before final building inspection, with quarterly maintenance records kept on site.
expected_conditions.basis: San Francisco FOG Control Ordinance requires grease-capturing equipment for every establishment with limited or full cooking; SFPUC assigns a Discharger Category and device type. The catalog entry states an undersized or missing interceptor commonly delays final DBI sign-off.

expected_conditions.condition: At least one owner or employee must hold a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe or equivalent) within 60 days of opening, and all food-handling employees must obtain California Food Handler Cards within 30 days of hire.
expected_conditions.basis: California Retail Food Code §113947.1 requires a certified manager for each food facility; §113948 requires a handler card for every employee who handles food. DPH inspectors verify the manager certificate at the pre-opening inspection.

filing_playbook.action: Request a written Letter of Determination from San Francisco Planning Department confirming zoning entitlement for the restaurant expansion at 1152 Taylor St.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Describe the existing Nob Hill Cafe with the 1981 Type 41 license, the proposed expansion into 2,290 sq ft, and ask: (1) Does the property qualify as a corner lot under §231 Limited Corner Commercial Use? (2) If not, does the expansion fall within the non-conforming use boundaries of the 1981 restaurant under §186, or does it require a Conditional Use Authorization? (3) What documentation of continuous operation since 1981 does Planning require to confirm non-abandonment? (4) Are operating hours before 10 p.m. principally permitted, or do they require CU review? Request the determination before investing in architectural plans or filing any permit applications.

filing_playbook.action: If Planning confirms the expansion requires a Conditional Use Authorization, file a CUA application with the Planning Department including a project description, floor plan, neighborhood outreach summary and environmental evaluation application.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Frame the restaurant as a neighborhood-serving use that continues a 40-year food-service presence at the site, emphasize limited cooking with no late-night hours, commit to a community liaison during construction, and describe the expansion as filling underutilized retail space in a low-density restaurant area (only 2 food businesses within 500 ft). Attend a pre-application meeting with Planning staff to confirm the filing is complete and whether neighborhood notification under §311 is required. Budget 5–8 months from filing to Commission hearing and decision.

filing_playbook.action: If Planning confirms the use is allowed as a continuation or corner-commercial use without a CUA, register the business with the SF Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN).
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File online or in person with the entity name, EIN, physical address, and business activity (restaurant). Pay the tiered registration fee based on projected SF gross receipts (e.g., $55 up to $100k for 2023). The BAN is required on every other city permit application, so complete this within 30 days of starting business and before filing the health plan check or building permit.

filing_playbook.action: Submit a Public Health plan check application to SF Department of Public Health Environmental Health Branch for the kitchen layout, equipment, finishes and menu, with two sets of scaled drawings.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Include the BAN, entity name, EIN, and a menu describing preparation methods for limited cooking. Show on the plans: three-compartment sink, hand sinks at cook and service stations, sealed flooring and wall surfaces, mechanical ventilation, refrigeration and dry storage. State that a certified food safety manager will be on staff before opening. Request that 'health' be added as a routing station on the linked building permit application so DPH and DBI review in parallel. Budget 3–8 weeks for plan review and expect one round of corrections.

filing_playbook.action: File a building permit application with the Department of Building Inspection for tenant improvements and change of use, with architectural plans stamped by a California-licensed architect and showing the approved DPH kitchen layout.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Describe the scope: limited cooking equipment, new partitions, electrical and plumbing for sinks and appliances, ADA-compliant restroom upgrades if needed, and change of use from retail to restaurant. Include the DPH-approved plan check and request routing to Planning for zoning referral under §175. If Planning required a CUA, attach the Commission's Motion and say the use is authorized by that decision. Licensed electricians, plumbers and mechanical contractors will pull separate permits for their trades. Budget 2–4 months for plan review and corrections before permit issuance.

filing_playbook.action: During construction, arrange with SFPUC Wastewater Enterprise for grease interceptor sizing and installation review, and file the Installation Verification Form before scheduling the final DBI inspection.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Contact the FOG program after the building permit is issued; SFPUC will assign a Discharger Category (1, 2 or 3) based on the kitchen size and menu, which dictates whether a passive grease trap or hydromechanical interceptor is required. Have the plumber install the device per SFPUC specs and photograph the installation. File the Installation Verification Form to qualify for the 14.2% sewer-bill discount, and keep quarterly maintenance logs on site for inspections.

filing_playbook.action: Two weeks before the planned opening date, schedule the final DPH pre-opening inspection online through the Environmental Health portal, and ensure at least one person has completed the Certified Food Protection Manager exam.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Confirm with your plan reviewer that the facility is at 100% completion: equipment installed and operational, all sinks plumbed with hot and cold water, walls and floors sealed, food stored six inches off the floor, and a certified manager certificate in hand. Walk the space against the DPH checklist before the inspector arrives. If the inspection passes, DPH will issue the permit to operate the same day or within 48 hours; if it fails, corrections must be completed and a reinspection scheduled at $276/hour, delaying opening by 1–3 weeks.

filing_playbook.action: File a sign permit application with SF Planning and DBI for any new exterior business signage, awning or illuminated sign, before fabrication or installation.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit a photo simulation or elevation drawing showing the sign's size, placement, illumination and materials. Planning reviews for compliance with Article 6 sign controls; in RM-3 districts signs are limited by frontage width and height, and internally illuminated signs may require additional review. Budget 2–6 weeks for approval of a simple storefront sign. Install only after the permit is issued to avoid a notice of violation and removal order.

timeline_cost.notes: No time or government cost is given because the zoning determination is insufficient information: the rules could not decide whether the restaurant use is allowed at 1152 Taylor St in RM-3 zoning without knowing if the property qualifies under Limited Corner Commercial Use (§231) or Limited Commercial Use (§186), and whether the expansion requires a Conditional Use Authorization. If a CUA is required, the timeline from pre-application meeting to Commission decision is typically 5–8 months (120–240 days) based on the 2015 precedent at 1030 Washington St which filed in May and was approved in November 2015 (189 days); CUA fees as of June 2023 started at approximately $2,700 for a no-construction case and scale with project cost. If the use is allowed as a continuation or corner-commercial use, the health permit, building permit and sign permit together take 2–5 months in parallel (building permit 14–120 days, health plan check and permit 35–105 days combined, sign permit 7–45 days) with government fees of approximately $2,100–$18,900 depending on construction valuation: health plan check $828–$2,207, health permit to operate $470, building permit $800–$15,000, and sign permit $300–$1,500. These ranges are for the city approvals only and assume the zoning question is resolved in the operator's favor; if the use is not permitted the concept as described cannot proceed at this address. State business and tax registrations (EIN, entity formation, seller's permit, business registration) add $125–$850 in fees and 1–4 weeks, completed in parallel at project start. Music licensing (ASCAP, BMI) adds $600–$5,000 annually but is not a government permit and takes 1–2 weeks to set up before opening.
